titleEn: God stands in the divine assembly
progression: | Em Em | C C | Am B7 | Em Em |
intro: Eight verses and a courtroom. God stands up inside an assembly, charges its members with judging crookedly, and sentences them to die like men. It is the psalm of the day for Tuesday. For a learner it is the cleanest drill in the book on one root: the verb for judging appears in verses 1, 2, 3 and 8 in four different forms, third person, second person plural, plural imperative and singular imperative, the root turning through the grammar while the psalm turns through its argument. Watch also who is speaking. Verse 1 is a narrator, verses 2 to 7 are God, and verse 8 is the psalmist answering from outside the room.

stichs.en: God stands in the assembly of God;
in the midst of the divine beings He judges.

verses.summary: The scene is set in one line: a standing figure, an assembly, and judgement happening inside it rather than over it. Everything that follows is spoken in that room.

stichs.en: How long will you judge unjustly,
and lift up the faces of the wicked? Selah.

verses.summary: The charge. Judging injustice and lifting faces are two ways of naming one offence: deciding by who is standing in front of you instead of by what happened.

stichs.en: Judge the weak and the orphan;
declare the afflicted and the destitute in the right.

verses.summary: The job description, delivered as commands, which means it was never unknown to them. Four categories, all of them people with nobody to lean on.

stichs.en: Rescue the weak and the needy;
deliver them from the hand of the wicked.

verses.summary: The second pair of commands moves from the verdict to the extraction. Judging correctly is not enough while the wicked still have hold of the person.

stichs.en: They do not know and they do not understand;
all the foundations of the earth are shaken.

verses.summary: An aside, and the only verse addressed to nobody. Bad judging is described as a failure of sight, and then the scale jumps: the earth itself loses its footing.

stichs.en: I said: You are divine beings,
and sons of the Most High, all of you.

verses.summary: The sentence opens by conceding the status. They really were called divine and sons of the Most High, which is what makes the next verse a demotion rather than an insult.

stichs.en: Nevertheless you shall die like a man,
and fall like one of the princes.

verses.summary: The verdict. Not that the title was false, but that it buys no exemption from the one thing they were appointed to protect other people from.

stichs.en: Arise, O God, judge the earth,
for You shall hold all the nations as Your inheritance.

verses.summary: The psalmist speaks for the first time since verse 1. If the appointed judges are being removed, the bench is empty, and the request is that God take the whole earth himself.

pardes.body: A trial in which the defendants are judges. Verse 1 is stage direction, verse 2 is the charge, verses 3 and 4 restate the neglected duty as four imperatives, verse 5 is an aside about their blindness and what it costs, verses 6 and 7 pass sentence, and verse 8 is the psalmist asking God to take the office over. Who stands in the dock is the psalm's open question, and the text does not settle it. Read one way, the elohim of {{1.7}} and {{6.2}} are human judges and the psalm is about corrupt courts. Read the other way they are members of a divine council, and the psalm is about God dismissing the powers set over the nations. Both readings are ancient and both are still held.

The root of judging runs through four forms: {{1.8}}, third person, He judges; {{2.2}}, second person plural, you judge; {{3.0}}, plural imperative, judge; {{8.2}}, singular imperative with the long ending, judge, this time addressed to God. The psalm is that root conjugated. {{2.4}} with {{2.6}} is the idiom for partiality, literally lifting the faces of the wicked, and it is the same pair of words that means showing favour when God is the subject and means corruption when a judge is. {{5.9}} has earth without the article and {{8.3}} has it with, which is the difference between foundations giving way somewhere and the whole earth changing hands. The hardest word is the one in {{6.2}}, since the identical form in {{1.2}} has to mean God himself: one noun, two referents, sometimes inside a single verse.

Verse 6 was also read as a statement about Israel rather than about judges. In that reading the words you are divine beings were said at Sinai, the status conferred there was real, and verse 7 records what happened when it was forfeited, so that dying like a man is a return to a condition that had briefly been lifted. The reading is traditional and it competes with the plain courtroom sense, which keeps the addressees on the bench from verse 1 through verse 7. What both readings share is a refusal to treat the title as empty flattery. The psalm does not say you were never gods. It says you will die anyway.

What the psalm shows collapsing is judgement without its counterweight. {{5.6}}, the verb used of the foundations, is the same verb the psalms use for a person being shaken, so the picture is the earth losing its footing the way a man does, and the cause named is not violence but bad courts. In the mystical idiom, strict judgement operating alone cannot hold a world together; it needs the side that gives without weighing first. Verse 8 is then not only a request for a better judge but a request for a different mode of judging, since the ground given is ownership rather than verdict: judge the earth, because it is already Yours.
